sections.title: The Impurity of the Hands
sections.html:
Netilat yadayim (ritual washing of the hands) is one of the seven mitzvot that the Sages instituted. In order to understand the root of their enactment, we must first explain that according to the Torah, the entire body is considered a single unit with regard to impurity and purity: either it is entirely pure or it is entirely impure. That is to say, if one of the limbs of the body touched one of the sources of impurity, then the entire body becomes impure. For example, if one touches a corpse with his foot, not only does the foot become impure, but the entire body becomes impure. Likewise, purification must include the entire body, and therefore when a person immerses in a mikveh in order to purify himself, he must immerse his entire body in the water at once.

In addition to this law, the Sages established that the hands have a special and separate status. Since they are occupied with all matters of action and physical matter, they become dirtier than the rest of the body, and they may also unintentionally touch impure things. Therefore the Sages established that ordinary hands are considered impure, and the way to purify them is by washing them with water (see Rashi, Shabbat 14a).

This enactment went through several stages. In the period of the First Temple, King Shlomo instituted impurity of the hands with regard to sacrifices: anyone who comes to touch a sacrifice with his hands must first purify his hands, and if he touched it without purifying his hands, he rendered the meat of the sacrifice impure and disqualified it from being eaten. In the period of the Second Temple, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel instituted that the hands are impure with regard to teruma as well: anyone who touches teruma without washing disqualifies it from being eaten, and in order that people not stumble by eating it, it must be burned (Shabbat 14). Afterward the Sages expanded the mitzva, and established that it is forbidden to eat bread without washing the hands (Ḥullin 106a).

Two reasons were given for the mitzva of washing before eating bread. The first is because of serakh teruma (a safeguard for teruma). That is to say, in order that the kohanim become accustomed to washing their hands before eating teruma, the Sages instituted that all of Israel wash their hands before a meal, and by having the custom of washing take root among all of Israel, the kohanim will be more firmly committed to washing their hands before eating teruma. And although today the Holy Temple is destroyed, and since there is no way to become purified from the impurity of a corpse, the kohanim have not eaten teruma for many generations, the enactment of washing has not been annulled, because we hope that the Holy Temple will soon be rebuilt, and we must be prepared for and accustomed to the practices of purity. The second reason is that the hands are busy, and in the course of this they touch filthy places, and it is not proper to eat with soiled hands. That is to say, in order to preserve the purity and holiness of eating, the Sages instituted washing the hands before a meal. And they based their words on the verse (Vayikra 11:44): "You shall sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy": "'You shall sanctify yourselves' — this refers to the first waters" (Berakhot 53b). Even one whose hands are clean, for example, he has just now washed them with water and soap, must wash his hands before eating bread, in order to purify and sanctify them in preparation for the meal (see SA OḤ 158:1; MB 1).

sections.title: The Spiritual Reason for the Mitzva
sections.html:
The more vital an activity is for a person, the greater its influence for good or for bad. Therefore, many laws were stated concerning eating, which is an important foundation of a person's existence. For it is possible to eat in order to satisfy a physical need and a momentary pleasure, and it is possible to eat in order to receive strength for a life full of content and meaning. And all the laws stated concerning matters of eating are meant to direct us so that eating will strengthen the good feelings within us and give us strength to rise up and engage in repairing the world, and will not debase our souls to a materialistic craving devoid of spiritual content. And since bread is the main food of a person, the Sages instituted washing the hands before eating it.

Most human actions are carried out by means of the hands and the fingers. The hands have the power to do good and beneficial deeds, and on the other hand, bad deeds. This is expressed in their unique capacity for movement: one can raise them above the head and one can lower them down. They grasp, touch and feel everything, and therefore they are liable to become dirtier than the other limbs. And since the purpose of the meal is to grant additional strength and vitality, we purify the hands from the filth that clung to them during worldly occupations, and sanctify them in preparation for the meal, so that we can draw from the food the vitality needed for a life full of values and content.

This is what the Sages said (Sota 4b): "Whoever eats bread without washing the hands, it is as if he had relations with a harlot." Both eating and the love between a man and a woman are very vital to a person's existence, and like everything in our lives, they can be done in holiness or, Heaven forbid, the opposite. And just as the Torah commanded that one not love by way of harlotry, but only through ḥuppa and kiddushin (marriage), so the Sages instituted that we wash our hands before a meal, and thereby we purify and sanctify our eating. But one who eats without washing, it is as if he eats impure bread, for he relates only to the physical aspect of the bread (Maharal, Netiv Ha-avoda 16).

The mitzva of washing applies to one who eats bread, and even if he will not touch the bread with his hands but will eat it with a knife and fork, or another person will feed him, he is obligated to wash his hands. But a person who does not intend to eat himself, even if he touches bread in order to feed another person, does not need to wash his hands. For the enactment of washing is meant to purify and sanctify a person in preparation for his eating, and therefore only one who is about to eat himself must wash his hands (SA OḤ 163:2).

sections.title: The Area That Must Be Washed
sections.html:
According to Rashi, the Rosh and many other poskim, the water of the washing must rinse all the fingers up to the place where they join the palm, but one does not need to rinse the palm. Whereas according to the Rif, the Rambam and other poskim, the obligation of washing includes the entire hand, from the tips of the fingers up to the place where the hand joins the arm.

And although according to the basic law it would be possible to be lenient, since the mitzva of washing is rabbinic, the halakha was ruled that it is proper to be stringent and wash the entire hand up to the place where it joins the arm. For it is explained in the Talmud (Shabbat 62b) that whoever treats netilat yadayim lightly comes to poverty, and Rav Ḥisda said about himself that he was accustomed to washing his hands with abundant water, and in this merit he attained wealth. Therefore, it is proper to be scrupulous and pour water abundantly over the entire hand, and not to be sparing and wash only the fingers (Beit Yosef and SA 161:4; and see BHL).

However, in pressing circumstances, when there is little water, or when there are wounds on the palm, one may rely on the lenient opinion and wash only the fingers and the knuckles, with a blessing (MB 161:22).

It is worth noting that all agree that one must wash the fingers; the dispute concerns the palm. The rule is that impurity clings more to the extremity of a person's body, and therefore it is clear that impurity rests on the fingers more than on the palm. The reason for this can be explained as follows: a person's inner self is pure, his inner will is directed toward the good, whereas the complications and impurity stem from the encounter with the outside world. Therefore impurity rests more on the extremity of a person's body, in the place farthest from the center of his body, from his heart, which alludes to the pure inner self within him.

The main destiny of a person is to contend with the outside world, to repair it and elevate it, and this role is actually carried out with the hands, through which he acts and does, gives and takes. But as a person goes out to contend with the outside world, he is liable to become soiled and defiled by the filth in the world. And this impurity clings to the fingers, which are the extremity of the body and which are occupied with worldly matters. And they disagreed whether the palm is also included in the extremity of the body that receives impurity, or perhaps only the fingers.1

sections.title: A Blessing over Rabbinic Mitzvot
sections.html:
Netilat yadayim is one of the seven mitzvot that the Sages instituted. And the Torah gave the Sages the power to establish mitzvot, as it is stated (Devarim 17:10-11): "You shall take care to do according to all that they instruct you," "You shall not turn aside from the word that they tell you, to the right or to the left." Therefore we recite over the washing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the washing of the hands." For although washing is not mentioned in the Written Torah, we were commanded to fulfill the enactments of the Sages.2

In principle, the mitzvot whose foundation is in the Written Torah are more important than the mitzvot that are rabbinic, and there is likewise a halakhic rule that in any case of doubt: if the source of the mitzva is in the Written Torah, one must be stringent, and if it is rabbinic, one is lenient. However, in a certain respect the words of the Sages are more beloved than the words of the Torah (Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:4). For the enactments of the Sages contain an expression of will on our part to add and take upon ourselves more mitzvot, in order to rise higher, to become sanctified and to draw closer to God.

One must know that because of the supremacy and holiness of the Written Torah, it is difficult for us to encounter the depth of its ideas and to keep its mitzvot. And in order that we be able to keep the Torah, God commanded the Sages to make a fence around the Torah and to issue decrees so that through them we will be able to keep all the mitzvot of the Torah. That is to say, the mitzvot of the Sages are a necessary bridge between a person and the Divine Torah, for these mitzvot express the Divine idea as it is received in this world, through the human understanding of the Sages of Israel.

So that people would not treat the words of the Sages lightly, the Sages sometimes reinforced their own words more than the words of the Torah (Eruvin 77a). And likewise it is related in the Mishna (Eduyot 5:6) that Elazar ben Ḥanokh cast doubt on the enactment of netilat yadayim, and the Sages excommunicated him. And when he died, the court sent and placed a stone on his coffin, for whoever dies while excommunicated, his coffin is stoned. It is likewise related in the Talmud (Eruvin 21b) about Rabbi Akiva, who in his old age was imprisoned by the Romans, and every day Yehoshua his attendant would bring him food and water for drinking and for washing the hands. One day the jailer spilled half of the water, so that there did not remain a sufficient amount for washing and drinking. Rabbi Akiva preferred to use that water for washing and not for drinking. And although according to the law, in such a situation of duress he was exempt from netilat yadayim, Rabbi Akiva preferred to be stringent with himself and almost endanger his life through thirst, as long as he would fulfill the words of the Sages who instituted washing the hands before a meal. Through his self-sacrifice Rabbi Akiva taught all of us how important it is to be meticulous in fulfilling the words of the Sages.

sections.title: Netilat Yadayim for Food Dipped in Liquid
sections.html:
As part of the enactment of netilat yadayim before eating bread, the Sages instituted washing the hands before eating food dipped in liquid. We will not enter into the details of the laws; we will only note that water or other liquids from the 'seven liquids' (wine, honey, oil, milk, dew, blood, water) cause the transfer and intensification of impurity. Therefore the Sages instituted that anyone who eats a fruit or other food that has moisture of one of the 'seven liquids' on it should wash his hands and thereby purify them, for otherwise, his hands would render the fruit or food impure.

According to most poskim, even today, when we do not observe the laws of impurity and purity, one must wash the hands before eating food that has one of the liquids on it. And just as the law of netilat yadayim before a meal has not been annulled in our times, so too the law of washing before eating food dipped in liquid has not been annulled. This is the opinion of the Rambam, Rashi, Rabbeinu Yona, the Rosh and others.

However, according to the Maharam of Rothenburg, the author of the Ittur and Tosafot (Pesaḥim 115a), there is a difference between the washings: the washing before bread was instituted also for the sake of holiness and cleanliness, and therefore also in our times one must sanctify the hands and clean them in preparation for the meal. But the law of netilat yadayim before food dipped in liquid is only because of serakh teruma, and since today the laws of impurity and purity are not observed, there is no need to wash the hands before eating food dipped in liquid.

Most Aḥaronim ruled that one should wash the hands before eating food dipped in liquid, but since some say there is no mitzva to wash, they instructed not to recite a blessing over this washing (SA 158:4; MB 158:20).

However, in practice, many are accustomed not to wash their hands before eating food dipped in liquid (Divrei Ḥamudot; Magen Avraham 158:8). This is because netilat yadayim is an enactment of the Sages, and consequently the law is that in a situation of doubt, such as a dispute among the poskim, the halakha follows the lenient opinion. Not only that, but in many cases of eating food dipped in liquid there is also a doubt whether, according to the stringent opinion, one needs to wash the hands, as explained in the note.3

sections.title: For What Quantity of Bread Must One Wash
sections.html:
The poskim disagreed on the question of for what quantity of food one must wash the hands. Some say that the law of netilat yadayim parallels the Ha-motzi blessing, and just as one who eats even a tiny piece of bread must recite Ha-motzi, so too he must wash his hands (Leḥem Ḥamudot and Magen Avraham). And some say that the washing was instituted for one who intends to eat the amount of a kezayit. According to this opinion, the law of netilat yadayim parallels the law of Birkat Ha-mazon, and just as one recites a final blessing over eating the amount of a kezayit, so too one who eats this amount must wash his hands before eating it (Ritva and the Gra). And some hold that there is room to say that netilat yadayim was instituted only for one who intends to eat the volume of an egg (kebeitza) (Beit Yosef, based on the Roke'aḥ).

As halakha, we take all the opinions into account; therefore, even one who intends to eat a tiny amount of bread should wash his hands. But only one who intends to eat bread in the amount of a kebeitza should recite the blessing, for this is the rule: in every doubt concerning blessings, the ruling is not to recite the blessing (SA 158:2-3; MB 10). Every person knows the size of an egg, and if in his estimation the bread he intends to eat has the volume of an egg, he should recite the blessing over the washing (see below 10:6).

One who intends to make a fixed meal (keviat se'uda) on baked goods of the Mezonot types must also first wash his hands with a blessing, and recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over them (as explained in MB 158:8; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 158:7; and below 6:2).

sections.title: The Water
sections.html:
The washing must be performed from a vessel containing at least a revi'it ha-log of water, which is like the volume of one and a half eggs (75 ml; below 10, note 11). One who washes with less than this amount has not fulfilled his obligation (below, halakhot 11-12).

The water must be clear, in its natural appearance, but if its appearance has changed, it is disqualified for washing. Accordingly, it is forbidden to wash the hands with juice, since it is water whose appearance has changed (SA OḤ 160:1).

Water with which work has been done is disqualified for washing, because through the work it has become like waste water. Therefore water in which dishes were rinsed is disqualified for washing. Likewise, water in which a hot bottle was placed in order to cool it and serve it to a baby is disqualified for washing, because work was done with it (SA 160:2).

In order to explain a little the purifying quality of water, we must first note that, as is known, impurity belongs to death and to non-existence, and therefore a corpse is the avi avot ha-tum'a (ultimate source of impurity). In contrast, water is the liquid of life, through which all kinds of plants and animals exist. Moreover, water preceded all of creation, for even before the beginning of the account of Creation it is stated: "and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the water"; it turns out that water is the primordial element. Therefore perhaps the Torah commanded that a person who has become impure and distanced from the source of his life should immerse his entire body in a mikveh of water, in the primeval element of life in the world, and through this the roots of life within him will be awakened, the pure soul within him will grow stronger, and the impurity that clung to his flesh will depart. In addition, it is the nature of water to clean the dirt that clung to the flesh, and there is a symbolism in immersion: just as dirt is cleaned and removed by water, so too the impurity that clung to a person's exterior passes and departs through immersion in water (see Peninei Halakha: Family Purity 1:11-12).

This reason also applies to the washing before a meal. Eating is liable to lower a person to the materialistic side, but when he first purifies his hands with water, which is the foundation of life, he elevates his eating to the ideal aim: that the food and its good taste give him strength and joy for a life full of content.

This is perhaps the reason that the Sages praised one who washes his hands with abundant water (Shabbat 62b). The intention is that he washes his hands in an enhanced manner, in such a way that the water rinses his entire hand. But they did not intend to encourage the one washing to waste a lot of water for nothing, for this involves the prohibition of bal tashḥit (wasteful destruction).

sections.title: A Vessel
sections.html:
The washing that purifies the hands in preparation for the meal must be performed by means of a vessel, just as we find that the kohanim would sanctify their hands and feet from the basin (kiyor), which is a vessel. Without a vessel, the washing is invalid. For example, if one's friend scooped up water in his palms and poured it onto his hands, he has not fulfilled the obligation of washing, because it was done without a vessel. Likewise, if he filled a plastic bag with water and poured water from the bag onto his hands, he has not fulfilled the obligation of washing, because the bag is not a vessel.

The vessel must hold at least a revi'it (one and a half eggs, 75 ml). If it does not hold this amount, it is invalid for washing (SA 159:1).

A vessel that has a hole in it, if the hole is kones mashkeh, that is to say, if it were placed in liquid, the liquid would enter it through the hole, it is invalid. And when there is water in it and it drips out of it drop after drop continuously, the hole is certainly of the size of kones mashkeh and it is invalid (SA 159:1; MB 7).

If the hole is wider and water comes out of it with which one can wash the hands, and up to the place of the hole the vessel holds a revi'it, the vessel is valid for washing through the hole (SA 159:2).

If there is a break in the rim of the vessel, one may still wash the hands with it, but one must take care to wash via the place where the rim is broken, because only up to the place of the break is the water kept in the vessel without overflowing, and what is above that, since it is not able to hold the water, is not considered a vessel and is invalid for washing. Likewise, it is permitted to wash the hands from a pitcher that has a spout on its rim, but if the spout is lower than its regular rim, one must wash via the spout. And likewise it is permitted to wash the hands from a kettle, but if its spout is lower than the rest of its rim, one must wash via its spout, because the kettle holds its water only up to this height (MB 159:24).

Some say that le-khatḥila one should not wash with a disposable cup made of plastic or cardboard, because it is not considered a lasting vessel, since one intends to throw it away after use. However, in practice, the opinion of most poskim is that there is no difference whether one uses a vessel once or several times, and since a disposable cup is also used as a vessel, for one drinks from it, it has the status of a vessel and it is permitted to wash the hands with it (Tzitz Eliezer 12:23). However, for the sake of hiddur mitzva (enhancing the mitzva), it is preferable to use a permanent vessel that one does not intend to throw away (Az Nidberu 6:48; and see Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 5, note 5).

It is permitted to wash the hands from a bottle, and although it may take a little time until the water wets the entire hand, there is no problem with this. If possible, it is preferable that the water flow continuously until it wets the entire hand (MB 162:30; see Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 27-28).

One can learn from this halakha that every idea or ideal, even if it is most exalted, needs a framework in order to be realized. The water symbolizes the content, and the vessel the framework, without which the water cannot purify the hands.

sections.title: Ko'aḥ Gavra and the Law of a Faucet
sections.html:
The Sages instituted that the water be poured onto the hands from a vessel, and that this pouring be done by ko'aḥ gavra, that is, by human force. And they based their words on the verse (Bemidbar 19:17): "and he shall put living water upon it in a vessel." But a person who wet his hands in the rain has not fulfilled the obligation of washing, because the water came onto his hands without a vessel and without ko'aḥ gavra.

For example, water urns that have a faucet at their bottom are considered vessels according to all opinions, and therefore a person may tilt the urn until the water pours from it onto his hands, and thereby fulfill the mitzva of netilat yadayim. The question is whether it is permitted to wash the hands by opening the faucet at its bottom. On the one hand, the water comes out through the force of the person who opened the faucet; on the other hand, his action only removed the stopper in the faucet, and the water flowed by itself, and the question is whether such an action is considered ko'aḥ gavra. As halakha, the water that comes out immediately after opening the faucet is considered water that came by human force, but what flows afterward is considered as flowing by itself, and one should not wash the hands with it. Therefore, one who wishes to wash his hands from the faucet of an urn must place his hand under the faucet, open it, and after the first water has come out of it, close it, and so repeat the same action until the water wets the entire hand, for it is possible to complete the washing of each hand with several consecutive pourings (SA 159:9; MB 162:30).

All this applies specifically to a faucet attached to a vessel, but one cannot wash the hands with the regular faucet in a sink, for although the first stream that comes out after opening the faucet is considered as coming from ko'aḥ gavra, the water pipe is not a vessel, and we have learned that the washing must come from a vessel.4

One may wash the hands without a vessel and without ko'aḥ gavra by immersing them in a kosher mikveh, and likewise in a spring, river or sea. For the power of a mikveh is greater than the power of washing, since immersion in a mikveh purifies the entire body, all the more so will it purify the hands. Over immersing the hands as well, one recites "al netilat yadayim" (see SA 159:14-20).

sections.title: Ḥatzitza (Interposition)
sections.html:
If dirt or paint stuck to one's hand, they interpose between the water and his hand. If the interposition covers most of the hand, it invalidates the washing.

But if the interposition is stuck to a minority of the hand, the law depends on whether people object to that interposition. If both he and most people are accustomed to object to that interposition, for example, there is paint on his hand that has substance, then even though it is on part of his hand, he must remove it before washing. And if he washed without removing it, his washing is invalid, and he should remove the interposition and wash his hands again with a blessing. Paint that has no substance, that is, which cannot be felt, even though people object to it, since it has no substance, does not interpose.

If the interposition stuck to a minority of his hand is an interposition that most people are accustomed to take care to remove but he does not object to it, or he takes care to remove it but most people do not object to it, he must remove that interposition before washing. And if he erred and washed with this interposition, he should wash again but should not recite a blessing, because according to some of the poskim, this is not an interposition.5

People whose work is painting, who regularly have stains of paint on their hands that are difficult to remove every day, even though other people are accustomed to object to such stains, for those who work with paint they are not considered an interposition, since it is known that they do not object to them. The same law applies to scribes of Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot (STaM) whose hands are stained with ink (SA 161:2).

Likewise, women who paint their nails, this is not an interposition, since they want it. But if the polish has begun to peel, and they are particular not to go about with it that way, it must be removed before washing.

A ring worn on the finger that one is not accustomed to remove in any situation is considered part of the hand and does not interpose for washing. But a ring that one takes care to remove at certain times is not considered part of the hand, and therefore it interposes for washing. Therefore, a woman who takes care to remove her ring when kneading dough must remove her ring before washing. And indeed according to the law, if it sits loosely on the finger, the water passes underneath it and consequently it does not interpose, but since it is sometimes difficult to tell whether it is loose or tight, the custom is to be stringent and remove before washing any ring that one is accustomed to remove at certain times (SA and Rema 161:3; Peninei Halakha: Family Purity 5:2, note 13).

One who was wounded on his hand to the point that he needed to stick a bandage or dressing on his wound, if he can easily remove the dressing and wash his hands, he should remove the dressing. But if this is painful for him, or removing the dressing would harm the wound, he should wash the rest of the hand, and thereby he fulfills the obligation of washing (SA 162:10). He should take care that the water reaches every place on the hand except the place under the bandage or dressing. And if he cannot wash the entire hand continuously, he should wash part of the hand each time with a revi'it of water (75 ml, as explained in the next halakha, that when one washes with a revi'it the water does not become impure).

A wound that has scabbed over: if the scab is bothersome and easy to remove, it should be removed before washing. But if it is not bothersome because of its small size, or it is difficult to remove because removing it might reopen the wound or cause pain, one does not need to remove it before washing (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 161:6; Peninei Halakha: Family Purity 5:14).

sections.title: The Order of Washing in Practice
sections.html:
This is the order of washing: first one washes the right hand twice in succession, and afterward one washes the left hand twice in succession. One begins with the right hand because it alludes to the attribute of ḥesed (kindness). Throughout the washing until the drying, the custom is to raise the fingers of the hands slightly. (Some are scrupulous, following the Arizal, to wash each hand three times, and afterward they raise the hands to the height of the head and recite the blessing; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 162:2.)

This washing differs from the morning washing, for in the morning washing one must wash each hand three times alternately, that is, right and then left, and so on in turn, until each hand has been washed three times. This is because after sleep, an evil spirit rests on the hands, and the Sages said that the way to remove it is specifically by washing alternately (Shabbat 109a). But in the washing for a meal, not only is there no need to wash alternately, but on the contrary, it is preferable to wash each hand twice in succession. For if it turns out that in the first washing he pours less than a revi'it (like the volume of one and a half eggs) on his hand, the first water that comes onto the hand will indeed purify the hand, but it itself (the water on the hand) will remain impure, and only through the second washing will the water on the hand also become pure. And in order to hasten their purification, people are meticulous to wash each hand twice in succession.

Although each hand is washed twice, it is right to take care to pour at least the amount of a revi'it ha-log (like the volume of one and a half eggs) on each hand the first time, and thereby one purifies the hands completely according to all the poskim.6

The common washing cup (natla) holds about a liter of water, and already with half of it one can perform the washing with all the enhancements. The problem is that many do not pour the water precisely and effectively, and so even when they pour a lot of water on the hand, they do not wet all the fingers and the palm, and consequently they do not purify the hand. Therefore one must learn to pour the water properly, so that in each washing the water reaches the entire hand.

It is worth noting that one may wash the hands with a regular cup. And although we take care to wash the entire hand and take care to pour a revi'it on each hand at the outset, and therefore the water in the cup is usually sufficient for only one hand, after finishing the washing of the right hand one may fill the cup with water from the faucet and continue washing the left hand. One need only take care, while filling the cup, that the washed hand does not touch the unwashed hand.

sections.title: Fine Points During the Washing
sections.html:
The process of removing impurity from the hands and purifying them is complex, and as long as it continues, one must be very careful not to spoil it. Therefore, after a person has washed his first hand, he must be careful not to touch it with his second hand. For if the unwashed hand touches the hand that has been purified, the unwashed hand will render impure the water on the pure hand, and that water will render impure both the hand that was purified and the unwashed hand. And since the impurity came to each hand from the other, there is no way to continue purifying them with an additional washing, because the additional washing can purify only the first water that became impure while purifying the hand, but water that became impure through contact with another hand is not purified by an additional washing; rather, one must dry the hands and begin the washing anew.

After completing the washing of both hands, that is, after washing each hand twice, they may touch each other, and many are accustomed to rub them against each other. But if another Jew whose hands are unwashed touches them with his hand, the hands become impure again, and in order to purify them one will need to dry them and begin the washing anew (SA 162:4; MB 45 and 48).

After the hands are dried, the process of their purification is sealed, and they no longer receive impurity. Even if another Jew who has not washed his hands touches them, the washed hands do not become impure. And even if that Jew's hand is wet, the washed hands, whose purification has already been completed, do not become impure, and he may continue the meal.

Some are meticulous to dry the handles of the washing cup of all moisture, because in their opinion, when a person takes the vessel for washing, the water on the vessel becomes impure from his hands, and after he washes his right hand and again grasps the handle in order to wash the left hand, the right hand will again become impure from the impure water on the handle. And in order to prevent the impurity of the water on the vessel, they dry the handles of the vessel of water (Pitḥei Teshuva and Shulḥan Shlomo).

But in practice, the opinion of most poskim is that one does not need to dry the vessel before washing. This is because only the water on the hands during the washing itself becomes impure from contact with an unwashed hand, but the water on the hands before the beginning of the washing does not become impure. For example, if one's hands were dirty and he rinsed them before washing, the water on his hands is not impure, and therefore without drying them he may fill the washing cup with water and wash his hands with it (BHL 162:2, s.v. "ha-noteil"). And likewise regarding the hand's contact with the handle of the washing cup: since it takes place before the beginning of the washing, the water on the handle does not become impure from the hand, and consequently also afterward, when in the course of the washing process the hand touches the water on the handle, the hand will not become impure from it. But one must be careful about one thing: to wash each hand twice in succession, for then the water on the hand becomes completely pure. But when one washes the hand once with less than a revi'it, the impure water on the hand passes to the handle, and when the second hand touches the handle, it becomes impure, and he will need to dry his hands again and wash them anew (MB 162:49; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 41).7

sections.title: The Time of the Blessing
sections.html:
One recites "al netilat yadayim" after the washing and before drying the hands. Seemingly one should ask: we recite the blessing over all mitzvot before performing them, in order to focus our intention in preparation for the mitzva, so why do we recite this blessing after performing it, that is, after the washing?

One reason is that sometimes it is not possible to say the blessing before the washing, because the hands are filthy and it is not proper to say the blessing with filthy hands, and therefore it is recited after the washing. And in order not to create confusion in the minds of those washing, the custom was established that everyone recites the blessing after the washing. Likewise we find that a righteous convert who immerses in order to convert recites the blessing over immersion after the immersion, because before the immersion he is still a gentile and cannot recite the blessing over the conversion (see Tosafot Berakhot 51a; Tur and Beit Yosef 158:11).

In addition, the drying is part of the mitzva, because it is repulsive to eat bread with wet hands, and the whole point of the washing is to purify and clean the hands in honor of the meal (Rashi, Sota 4b; MB 158:45-46). Accordingly, as long as one recites the blessing before drying, he is still considered as reciting it before the completion of the mitzva.8

Since the blessing refers to the entire process of washing, it is forbidden to interrupt with speech throughout the time from the beginning of the washing until the end of the drying. One should hurry to recite the blessing immediately after the washing, and likewise one should be quick to dry immediately after finishing the blessing.

sections.title: An Interruption Between Drying the Hands and the Ha-motzi Blessing
sections.html:
The poskim disagreed on the question of whether it is permitted to speak between finishing drying the hands and the Ha-motzi blessing. According to the Rambam, as long as one does not divert his attention from the fact that he is about to eat, he may speak about anything in the world, and this is not an interruption. But one who diverted his attention, through words or actions, to the point that he forgot that he is about to eat, has lost the washing and must wash his hands a second time. According to the Rosh, one should not interrupt with speech between the washing and the Ha-motzi blessing, and one may speak only for the needs of the meal; for example, if he is missing salt, a knife or bread, he may ask that they be brought to him.

In practice, the poskim wrote that it is proper to be stringent not to interrupt between drying the hands and the Ha-motzi blessing with speech that is not necessary for the needs of the meal (SA 166:1; MB 2-3). However, it is permitted to answer "Amen" at that time (Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh 41:2). Likewise, if an important person addressed him with a question, and if he does not answer him it would be an affront to his honor, he should answer him briefly.9

Some say (Rema, based on Tosafot Sota 39a) that it is proper that the time between finishing the washing and the Ha-motzi blessing be less than the time it takes to walk 22 amot, about 11 meters. But if the sink is 11 meters away from the table, one may wash the hands there le-khatḥila, and this is not an interruption. For the stringency is not to interrupt needlessly for the time it takes to walk 11 meters, but when it is needed, even according to the stringent opinion this is not considered an interruption (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 166:2).

sections.title: One Who Washes His Hands After Relieving Himself
sections.html:
Sometimes a person relieves himself before the meal, and it turns out that when he leaves the bathroom he must wash his hands for two reasons: first, to purify himself after relieving himself, and second, in preparation for the meal. The question is whether one washing is sufficient.

Some say that it is preferable to wash his hands twice. For if he washes once, he will need to recite two blessings at once, Asher Yatzar and Al Netilat Yadayim. Immediately after the washing he cannot recite Asher Yatzar, because it is forbidden to interrupt between the washing and the blessing over the washing, and even after he dries his hands he cannot recite Asher Yatzar, so as not to interrupt between the washing and the Ha-motzi blessing over the bread. And to postpone the Asher Yatzar blessing until after he begins to eat is too great a postponement. Therefore he should first rinse his hands without a vessel, in a manner that is not valid for netilat yadayim for a meal, and recite Asher Yatzar. Afterward, without needing to dry his hands, he should wash them a second time with a vessel, and recite the blessing over the washing (see SA OḤ 165:1 and MB 2).

And some say that one washing from a vessel is sufficient: before drying his hands he recites the blessing over the washing, and after drying his hands he recites Asher Yatzar, and afterward he recites the blessing over the bread and eats. In their opinion, the Asher Yatzar blessing is not considered an interruption between the washing and eating the bread. One who wishes to rely on their words may do so (see MB 165:2). And according to several of the great Aḥaronim, this custom is preferable, and so too many are accustomed (the Gra; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 165:2).

sections.title: One Who Relieves Himself in the Middle of the Meal
sections.html:
A person who in the middle of his meal touched a covered place on his body, where there is a little sweat, must wash his hands anew, because the aim of the washing is to clean and sanctify the hands in preparation for the meal, and when he touched a soiled place on his body, he lost the washing. According to many, one must even recite a blessing over this washing (Rashba; SA 164:2), but since there are those who disagree with this, he should wash his hands without a blessing (Maharshal; Knesset Ha-gedola). Even if he relieved himself (urinated), when he comes out he should wash his hands without a blessing.

But if he defecated, and he intends to continue eating more bread in the volume of an egg, he should wash his hands with a blessing. And this is what he should do: immediately after the washing he should recite Al Netilat Yadayim, and after drying his hands he should recite Asher Yatzar. And although there are those who have doubts about this too, this is the opinion of most poskim, and this is also the custom of many (MB 164:13, and BHL s.v. "laḥazor").10

If one went away from the place of the meal for an hour or more and diverted his attention from guarding his hands, even though he intended to continue eating bread, his law is like one who begins eating anew, who must wash with a blessing; but he should not recite Ha-motzi, since he intended to continue eating bread.11

sections.title: Pressing Circumstances
sections.html:
A person who wishes to eat bread and has no water for netilat yadayim, the Sages obligated him to go up to a distance of a mil (close to a kilometer, about 18 minutes' walk) in order to fulfill the mitzva of netilat yadayim. But if the water is farther than the distance of a mil, he should wrap his hands in a cloth or gloves, in order to interpose between his hands and the bread, and recite Ha-motzi and eat (SA 163:1).

One who is traveling and knows that there is water at a distance of several kilometers further along his route, if the water is closer than four mil (close to 4 km, about 72 minutes' walk), he must continue on his way, and when he reaches the water he should wash his hands and eat. And if the water is to the sides of his route or behind him, as long as it is at a distance of less than a mil, he should go to the water and wash his hands.

But if the water is farther than four mil ahead of him, or more than a mil to his sides, and he is hungry, he may wrap his hands in gloves or a cloth and eat without netilat yadayim. And if he has no cloth with which to wrap his hands, he should eat the bread with a fork or a spoon, so as not to touch the bread with his hands (see Rema 163:1; MB 7).12
